utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I take it that you're informed by Mr. Josse about the problems concerning the arrival and testimony of Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. In fact, I was informed pretty much straight away yesterday afternoon but in the circumstances it still wasn't feasible for us to get together and resolve all that yesterday. So thank you for the opportunity of considering it overnight. Your Honour, the Defence position is that we -- we are -- we are unwilling, we do not wish, please, to give up any of that valuable time between the 4th of April and the date the 11th on which the Trial Chamber is expecting Mr. Krajisnik to begin his evidence. So that really is -- that, we hope, gives the Trial Chamber, well, helpful steer on where the Defence stands in relation to Mr. Bjelica. As far as Mr. Bjelica's arrival is concerned, on examination, that letter from Bosnia and Herzegovina is clearly not saying that there is any non-compliance with the conditions for a 90 bis order. It is clearly not saying that Mr. Bjelica cannot be brought here because at the end of the letter the offer is really very clearly made, that if this Trial Chamber maintains the 90 bis order then he will be brought here. Your Honour, Mr. Josse indicated yesterday some of the extremely unsatisfactory aspects of videolink from the Defence point of view. Mr. Josse's position as described yesterday remains the position this morning, and I've also had an opportunity of talking briefly to Mr. Krajisnik before Your Honours came into court. He also is against the videolink of this witness. So I put that in the scales, Your Honour, it is a point. So our position is that, Your Honour. We do not wish, please, to give up that valuable time in early April, and we do not wish Mr. Bjelica to be dealt with by videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, isn't there an English saying that you can't have your cake and eat it? I'm wondering because there are two problems. The first problem is whether we could get Mr. Bjelica here in such time that -- that he could be examined before the 4th of April. And at the same time that in your schedule I see no further room for any further witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the Trial Chamber's schedule, Your Honour, in effect. Yes. "You can't have your cake and eat it" is an English phrase not often applied in trials of this nature but it does apply from time to time. Your Honour, that is the position. I can't disagree with what Your Honour says. In the schedule, in the Trial Chamber schedule which we are operating with Your Honour is quite right. There is no place for Mr. Bjelica as things stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's the first problem. And the second problem, if you would if you would refrain from another witness or if you would refrain from taking time. You say you would prefer not to do that. I understand that's where you want to have the cake and eat it. You would like to have an extra piece of cake. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to -- please, with respect, Your Honour, I'm not going to adopt that phrase in relation to the Defence's position at all. Your Honour may take whatever view Your Honour wishes as to cakes and eating. I'm just -- I state the Defence's position, Your Honour, and I'm not going to accept with respect any labels about cakes to what we're saying. The position, Your Honour, is this: That I haven't -- well, I've considered. I've had a chance to consider and I've taken that chance myself whether whatever the practicality is of getting Mr. Bjelica here, whether another witness should move out to make room for Mr. Bjelica. But, Your Honour, that is something which I certainly would need to discussion with Mr. Krajisnik for more than a couple of minutes which we have the opportunity to do as we come into court in the morning. That's a -- that is a technical possibility, Your Honour. I say no more than that. Of course it is. I don't know whether Mr. Bjelica could be got here as the earliest possible date. I simply don't know that at the moment. It's obviously not Monday or Tuesday, so the next witness isn't going to move over for Mr. Bjelica, but there aren't all that many candidates anyway as -- in the time frame up to the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, during the next break the Chamber will have an another look to the calendar. I announced already that there is a small chance that the Chamber will grant a couple of days extra for very specific reasons. The schedule has to be changed for other reasons as well since on the 29th of March, next Wednesday, there is a Plenary. And although we did our utmost best to move to another moment or we even asked permission not to attend the Plenary but that's not permitted, that means that we are not sitting next Wednesday anyhow, so that the 4th will most likely become the 5th or even the 6th or the 7th. We will inform you, keeping in mind your wishes. We'll inform you after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And it's extremely helpful to have advance notice about next Wednesday. We're grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other procedural matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not from me, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we meanwhile received the 65 ter summary in relation to Mr. Krsman. Mr. Josse, I couldn't say that all my concerns in relation to what I said yesterday have disappeared by reading the whole of it. It's again -- the Chamber finds crimes committed by other parties in the conflict not without significance, but the attention to be paid to it should be limited unless there's a good legal reason to raise the issue. I mean, we all know that tu quoque is not an issue. That's one. The second is that the Prosecutor who prosecutes crimes committed by all nationalities before -- not before this Chamber but before the Tribunal does not dispute from what I understand that serious crimes are committed by other parties as well, and perhaps even as we recently heard, crimes perhaps even committed in proximity, in proximity of the crimes that were committed allegedly in this case. Is that a correct reflection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, therefore, apart from the importance of learning how people, how the population may have reacted to what happened to them, that that is not the core of the case, although not -- I wouldn't say not unimportant, not irrelevant, but it's not the core of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, had predicted my response in effect. The Chamber allowed the Prosecution to call evidence from a number of sources about the suggestion that Mr. Krajisnik encouraged Serbs leave Sarajevo after Dayton. In our submission, the evidence of these brutal civilian killings supports the proposition that it was a spontaneous decision by the Serb population of Sarajevo to leave after Dayton in part because of the way they had been treated by their Muslim neighbours, and we submit that, bearing in mind the evidence, this Chamber allowed the Prosecution to call on that not unimportant issue, we, the Defence, are allowed to explore exactly how Serbs in Sarajevo were treated by their Muslim neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is aware that -- that this is part of the Prosecution's case, that Mr. Krajisnik encouraged Serbs to leave after Dayton. At the same time, again I got the impression, but please correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Tieger, that this specific aspect is of a relatively marginal importance for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that accurately characterises the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse, perhaps it could get the attention, the time which is in balance with the importance of that aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as Your Honour rightly reminded me yesterday, Your Honours run this case and Your Honours are going to decide this case. If Your Honours say to the Defence that this is not an issue of any importance whatsoever, then we will not pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, with respect, to say that something is of marginal importance to the case does not help the Defence one jot in this regard. It simply is a meaningless expression, I submit. Proper guidance as to where this issue lies is fine. In other words, if the Chamber says it's not going to be held against Mr. Krajisnik, it's not a consideration, it's not a factor, you the Defence don't need to worry about it, that's fine. But otherwise, Your Honour, I submit the expression "marginal importance" is simply meaningless, nebulous, and not really very fair to us in how we consider how to tackle the body of evidence that the Prosecution presented against our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it is all a matter of balance. It's the same as if you'd spent a lot of time to some events in some places and says if it's not held against us then we'll not deal with it, but otherwise we'll spend ten days of evidence on that, because at this part of the Prosecution's case. So fundamentally we do not disagree, but we know that we're talking about events during approximately two years in well over 30 municipalities. That requires to prioritise, to spend more attention to this aspect, to spend more attention to that aspect. The Chamber had the impression that this was a matter which the balance of the whole of the events should not take, well, let's say 20 per cent of the time. And if I said margin, of course, everything that is in the margin is still there, is still part of that case, but it's a matter of finding a balance on spending time more or less on this or on another matter. And I sought confirmation with the Prosecution to see what place this element took in their case. Of course, if you'd say this element, that's for the Defence really of such importance that we'd rather spend more time on that than anything else, entirely you're free to do it. But your time is limited, and therefore why a profound reflection on what is most important and less important needs to be done, and I leave that to the Defence because it's finally not this Chamber but you and your responsibility to Mr. Krajisnik which is determining to spend time on what. I just wondered whether the Chamber would find this element of such importance that it would spend major part of its judgement on this matter or that it would get a place in the whole of the case, which is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I imagine we say we wonder that as well, Your Honour, but I don't suppose the Court is going to help us with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course -- Mr. Josse, you couldn't expect us at this moment to express any -- it's just a first impression of elements, of aspects of the case, and I can imagine that the Defence is struggling with the issue, the issue of -- to spend how much time on what aspects of the case, to go into detail on point A and to go less in detail on point B. The Prosecution has to do it. I think the Defence, since time is not unlimited, will have to do the same. I'll ask Madam Usher to call the witness into the courtroom, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just express my appreciation of the switch to Monday afternoon which has been most helpful. I know that took quite a lot of organising and is much appreciated by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krsman. I'm afraid your headphones are going to fall off if you keep it that way. Yes. Mr. Krsman, please be seated. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, and before I give the opportunity to Mr. Josse to continue his examination if chief, Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question that -- [no interpretation]. [In English] -- numbered 10.000 inhabitants of Muslim ethnicity. Most of their housing was illegal little constructed. [Interpretation] In the following paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand there are problems with the translation. One second, please. Mr. Registrar, have the translation issues been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the position was, Your Honour, that I didn't have my headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was listening to it. I heard the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has it been resolved by now? Okay. I do understand that the matter has been resolved, so we'll ask Judge Hanoteau --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- makes a comment, Your Honour, because from this limited area I have some advantage over my co-counsel. The witness doesn't know what a 65 ter summary is with respect, Your Honour, so it is a little bit disconcerting to be thrown straight into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm only getting the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you on the right channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As Mr. Stewart indicates. Channel 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Should be English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We are on channel 4 and we are getting French, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm on channel and I get English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart's French is better than mine, sadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm experiencing precisely the same --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the interpreter apologises but the system was set up on channel 9 for English, that's why, in the French booth. That goes both way, which is why there was a problem. Now it's okay. I'm on channel 4 four English, so Judge Hanoteau can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a complicated start. I'm sorry about that, but -- it was a bit tedious but we'll get there. So yesterday you mentioned a change in the people's make-up in their population's make-up, something that was -- something that you could really see at the beginning of the war. We were told, if I remember right, I think you said there were about 20.000 Muslims who suddenly settled in an area that used to be with a Serb majority. And this is my question: Why was there this change in the population make-up composition? So did those Muslims come to settle in that area? Was it because there were factories that were set up, there was a need for labour? I'd like to know exactly why these people came, these Muslims came.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness. Microphone for the witness. It's on now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Krsman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sudden boom and increase in the number of Muslims was aimed at changing the structure between the ratio of Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, as well as a huge pressure on the Serb population to become more dominant through work, through our enlargement, because we Serbs could not obtain licenses to build houses. I personally, and my father who had two sons, me and my brother, we could not obtain a licence to build a house on our plot of land on which we had lived for 500 years, and they could build illegally and nobody pays the problem to them. Sarajevo is a big town. These people came from elsewhere. At that time, we did not see that as a political problem. However, the war proved that this was a political move aimed at destroying us as a people. However, they did not succeed, thank God. They succeeded in another way, and that was after the Dayton Accords when we all moved out. And I hope that the situation is now clear, that my answer was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This answer is very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, when we broke off yesterday, you were telling the Chamber about the collection of weapons from the Rajlovac barracks in approximately March of 1992. You've described how that happened. You had mentioned that it was implemented by a Colonel Miletic. And in addition to that, you had mentioned that the agreement to do this had been brokered by the Crisis Staff of both communities. Could you give some more details about how it was agreed, firstly the Serbs should collect some firearms and thereafter the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The condition for -- for this was our closeness. My house was next to a Muslim house, and our village was next to this Muslim village. The next reason for this agreement was the fact that Mr. Krajisnik lived in Zabrdje and because of good neighbourly relations and his persistence, insistence that this should happen. We lived with the local Muslims who had arrived there in the '70s, and we had agreed this arrangement, and we agreed something else which we implemented. We took explosives from the barracks, and we planted mines between us and them in the length of five kilometres for safety and security reasons, so as to prevent the extremists from doing that possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you because that's going ahead a little bit in the narrative I was going to ask you about in a moment's time. Was the implementation of the agreement that I'm interested in, not so much the implementation, but who brokered the community between the communities that the weapons in the barracks should be shared?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was agreed by the Crisis Staffs in agreement with the barracks commander, Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And who decided which firearms and other weapons should go to which community, and how many particular guns or whatever each community was entitled to?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every community received as much as they had able-bodied men. We received 202 rifles because that's how many we were. They were more numerous, and they received more than 800 rifles. We received only light weapons because there were no heavy weapons in the barracks. At that point, we never imagined that there could be an escalation of the conflict and that we would have to use heavy weaponry. Even the light weaponry was just a deterrent, and it was to be returned to the barracks like it was done after manoeuvres that had been organised in the past. And this is the way the Territorial Defence was organised in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the against you gave a few moments ago, you begun to tell the Chamber that after the weapons had been collected a minefield was laid between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we go to that, of course I'm addressing you, I know that the witness has no 65 ter, I noticed and I would like you to explore on that matter since it seems very much the core of the answer of the witness that there was an unbalance, 202 against 806 which he explains by saying that there were 202 able men. The 202, at least in the 65 ter summary, from the witness's village, that's at least what the 65 ter summary says, we also heard that the village was almost purely Serb and at the same time the 806 appears. I wonder what that number covered, the village only? Could you please explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I will happily do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I at the next convenient moment address the Court about the 65 ter in general? I'm quite happy to deal with Your Honour's issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- because, if I might say, it's a sensible one and one I'd like to pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the 202 men of Serb ethnicity who received firearms, where exactly did they come from?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these men resided in Zabrdje. Out of a thousand inhabitants, there were 202 able-bodied men. The rest were women and children who did not fall under any military obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about those of Muslim ethnicity, the 800-odd firearms? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all from Sokolje. The only difference between them and us is their families are more numerous. I worked during the census, and I know that each of them had four or five or even more children. Out of some 10.000 inhabitants, about 800 of them were able-bodied men, and those were the people who received weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why were the villages of Zabrdje and Sokolje the two villages that were selected to receive those weapons? Why not other villages, for example, the west side of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question. I only know and I can tell you that we were the closest. Our village was the closest to the separation line, and that is why we were chosen. And I can't tell you anything about other areas or other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I move on to the laying of the minefield. You'd begun to give some evidence about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Josse, of course you've explored that as I asked you to do. At the same time from arithmetics it's still very complicated because 800 able-bodied men on a population of 10.000 makes families of an average of 11 persons or 10 or 11 persons which is not consistent with what the witness told us where he said that the families were larger, three, four, even more children. To make that an average of 9 or 10 persons a family is quite surprising. That means that the explanation from a point of view of arithmetics in particulars is not very satisfactory. If you say, well, I'm not going to explore that any further, but it leaves an opportunity open that on an average -- well, family size -- well, let's say six persons a family which makes every family five -- four children as an average, then I still would have at least -- I would have 1.600 fathers. And, of course, it depends on where children are not children any more, but it's -- it's still rather vague and not entirely clear to me. I leave it up to you whether you want to further explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the best I can do is you've heard what the learned Judge has to said and I see you nodding, Mr. Krsman. Perhaps you could deal with the point he has just raised.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With pleasure. I was the president of the commission for census in 1991 in Rajlovac municipality, and I was also in charge of the census in Sokolje. In that village there were households and addresses where up to 20 people were registered. In that village, there were over a thousand pupils and students who had arrived from Sandzak, Zepa, Srebrenica, who were educated in Sarajevo, who were students in Sarajevo and were not military conscripts. They were just registered at those addresses. And that is why the number was so huge, 10.000, although not all 10.000 of them and resided there all the time. They didn't work there all the time. There were also a lot of elderly people who had sold their property in their places of origin, and then they built houses in Sokolje and registered as residents of Sokolje. I'm sure that 806 of them received rifles, and I know. I witnessed that, that this is certainly the number situation that was present in Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That explains at least to some extent the -- the problems I had. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What exactly did you witness? Which part of this procedure of taking weapons from the barracks did you witness?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally with ten persons from Zabrdje and ten persons from Sokolje took the explosives and together we planted the area between Sokolje and Zabrdje. We planted the mines and we went into the depth of our territory. We planted mines across my property. We did not want to go to the separation line, but we moved a bit further towards our side in order to gain trust and demonstrate that we were not plotting any attack on our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did the mines that you planted come from?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from the Rajlovac barracks depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the inhabitants of Sokolje plant any mines as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Not before that time. And afterwards, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In an answer you gave earlier, you said that this was done for safety and security reasons so as to present -- I beg you pardon, so as to prevent the extremists from doing that possibly. What extremists were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that in Zabrdje there was nobody who had come from elsewhere, but we knew very well that in Sokolje there were people who did not wish well to our state, who had come from elsewhere and wanted to create a problem, and that is why we agreed all that. And our fears were proven during the war. Throughout the war we remained united. Nobody ever came to our help. And as for them, they were helped by all sorts of people. And I'm sure there were other sorts of people who were better suited to approve that. I'm not the best suited, and it is not my intention to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you be given the map that was presented yet that hasn't yet been given a number. Could you be given a black pen, and could you mark where you planted the minefield, please.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The black line is the line on which mines were planted, the whole line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How long did it take you to complete that task?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very delicate job, and we did not have enough professionals. It took us three days to plant all those mines. Every day when we planted a certain quantity of mines, we secured those mines until we completed the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I ask one clarification? Mines are now dealt with after the weapons being given to both Serbs, 200, and 800 Muslims. You told us that that was agreed upon. This planting mines, was that part of an agreement as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this agreement -- was it an oral agreement or has ever anything been put on paper, are you aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an oral agreement, and we signed a receipt for all the weapons and the mines that we got from the barracks. We did it. Each of us did it for ourselves, both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When it was mutually agreed that these mines would be planted, why did your people plant them, or did you do it together with the Sokolje Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We planted the mines. The Muslims from Sokolje agreed to that, and they supervised us from a distance of some 50 to a hundred metres. We did not encounter a single problem. There were no incidents during that job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was an incident in Bjelice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, are you referring to Bjelice or -- because Bjelica is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Bjelice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we've found it on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incident was not in Bjelice but close to the Bozica gas station at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Using the pointer, show the Chamber where the Bozica gas station is?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, where it reads "17."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me give you this map as well, please. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, first of all, I think that the coloured map has not received a number yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D153. And then looking at this other map, that's a map which is already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the -- it's related to the testimony we heard about Ahatovici, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct. And it's -- I'm grateful again to my learned friends who prosecute. They provided us with a coloured copy of the map that's been marked. I could give the exhibit number. I think it may be D364, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Or even 386. I'm not sure. But the problem is, Your Honour, that map is heavily marked and clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want even to put that map in front of the witness. What in fact has happened, there's no secret, Mr. Krajisnik very helpfully has provided me with that map he must have been given at the time that evidence was called. He hasn't marked it, and that's why we're using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you could present it to the witness and give it another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's helpful I'm advised that that's P386.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just have that map back for one moment, Madam Usher, please. I'm wrong. They're not identical. I suspect, Your Honour, they are from the same map, but they are different -- they cover different areas. 386 and this map cover slightly different areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In other words, they're different extracts from the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, most important is that we find the map on which the gas station can be located.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take whatever one. And I think marking with numbers is -- I don't know of course. Perhaps it's not of major importance at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other suggestion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How important is it to know exactly the location? Is that of vital importance?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not, but what we do have is we have a black and white copy of 386 that has not been marked. Perhaps we could use that and I have lots of copies of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do what you wish, and also keep in mind if the location is not of vital importance, we could -- Mr. Registrar, this black and white map would receive --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, using the marker, the black marker, could you show us where the petrol station is?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the petrol station was on the main road from Vogosca towards Sarajevo. So that's the main road I'm talking about under Brijesce hill, exactly at this point here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Put a cross there or a -- it may be the learned Judge would rather you put a number. Just wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd make that -- well, could we give a letter which adds G for gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: P for petrol station, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, P for petrol station. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we zoom in so we know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. What happened there, please, Mr. Krsman?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that event accelerated the escalation of the conflict in our parts to a great extent, and the extremists on the Muslim side, in seeking a reason to violate the truce and agreement, they said that there were Chetniks at the petrol pump, and they set an ultimatum as far as I know that all the weapons should be handed over from the Rajlovac barracks, and then they attacked this Bozica pump because they made up -- that up from these rear portions around Sokolje. And there was fighting there and some people were killed and others wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in the month of March. Yes, March. From the 15th to the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was this before or after the collection of the weapons from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the weapons were collected from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when did this happen in relation to the laying of the minefield?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also after the mines were planted and according to our knowledge, once they'd seen at that there were weapons in the barracks they wanted to put an ultimatum in that way and to be able to seize the other weapons that were certainly still in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to move on. Mr. Krsman, as far as you are concerned, when did the war start in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war in Rajlovac started exactly on the 8th of May, and the frontal attack came from all sides, from all axes along the edges of my village, Zabrdje, and the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to deal with that in a moment. What I'd like you to tell the Chamber about before we deal with that attack is your state of readiness, the Serb state of readiness. What had your preparations been like? What were your weapons like, that sort of thing, on the eve of the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very fact that we did not have a single trench dug and that all of the population, the women and children still lived in Zabrdje, and that we had no plan for evacuation or anything like that in case of attack and that we only had those 200 rifles speaks for itself, tells you whether we thought it would be something serious and whether or not the crisis would escalate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that point was anyone living in the barracks as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this attack at the pump, at the petrol station in Bozica, all the Serb inhabitants who lived along the road, if the Trial Chamber still has the map before them, so all the inhabitants living along this road here were Serbs by ethnicity, and they moved to the barracks. They left their homes to the mercy of the Muslims because they were afraid that what happened at Bozic petrol pump would be repeated. And I would say that that meant about 200 inhabitants because there were about 50 to a hundred Serb households, perhaps a little more. In order to seek protection and safety there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Using the map, if it helps, show what military activity started the fighting on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map you can see -- or, rather, on the previous main showed you where we had planted the mines, but here you can see that they attacked the entire area along the separation line. This is where my house is, this is the exact point last point, the last black dot up there. And the mortar shells killed my next-door neighbour when they fell. And on that particular day, over 50 mortar shells fell on the village, and we had one casualty. One person was killed and two people were lightly wounded. My brother and I pulled out our children, and we never returned to the house again. As far as the Rajlovac barracks is concerned, they targeted all the buildings you can see here, and there are 20 to 30 of them, and the attacks were most fierce where the arms depot was located. And according to what we learnt later on, the Muslims who were officers in the Rajlovac barracks were in charge of the shooting operation and they became commanders later of companies, battalions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you learn that the Muslims in charge of the barracks were involved in the initial shooting operation?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the communications were still working at that time and some of our officers who were down there and stayed there for those ten days until the 15th of May told us that they were people who had served their -- done their military service in the Rajlovac barracks, and when I collected up the weapons I personally saw six Muslims who were down there, who were still down there in the army doing their regular military service, and they left before the 8th of May. They left Rajlovac barracks before the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned your neighbour who was killed. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Boro Bjelica, and he was killed exactly in front of his house, on his property, before the eyes of his two small children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Mr. Bjelica - I imagine I can lead on this - was in fact president of the local SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he was -- the place is called Bjelice as you saw on the map, and this was named after him because he was president of the SDS and he was a man who could rally people together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, was the fact that he was killed a coincidence or was it deliberate because of the position that he held or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't believe that it was deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you just say that Bjelice was named after this particular individual?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not by this particular individual but probably his ancestors, his grandfather or great grandfather. You have another village like Lemezi. This takes the name of the family that lived there for many, many years, hundred of years. So that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the matter. I'm not sure I've asked you this: Approximately how many people do you think were living in the barracks as of the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 8th of May -- well, on the 8th of May, there were just a few officers and their families who had in the succeeded in evacuating, and some of the civilians also who were working in the Rajlovac barracks. After the 8th of May, every day, every single day quite literally, civilians turned up who were fleeing Muslim torture from parts of Sarajevo where the Muslims were the majority population and from the areas under Muslim control, and this number varied from several hundred to several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned that your -- you and your family had to evacuate your house. Why was it that you were unable to return? And it may seem a silly question, but I think I should ask it.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unable to return for a very simple reason. My house was up at the front line. And not only my own house but my relatives' houses as well. And that meant that all the houses and people living up at the front line had to leave their homes not to lose their lives, quite simply. And we didn't dare risk that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did your wife and children go?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As my mother through force of circumstance was born at Pale, my relatives and family went to stay with my uncle at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you go there with them?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single able bodied man left in those first two or three months. And later on, very few people escaped or deserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the attack that you have described, how did you set about defending yourself?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: It was a terrible shock. We just couldn't believe that anything like that could happen. And since we didn't have a single trench in the village let alone any communicating trenches or any military formations of that kind and we didn't have any able-bodied men either that would be capable of setting up a defence line, we had to withdraw quite literally 500 metres into the depth of our territory and along the main road going through the village, and we left this space as no man's land which about one kilometre in length.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What -- in the first month of the war, tell it us about the military formation in Rajlovac on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, all you had in Rajlovac were high-ranking military officers who were professors, and their families, and there were the guards or, rather, a unit, I didn't know how many men it numbered, which provided security for the barracks, and they were there until the 15th, 16th or 17th, or rather, I know that the commander Miletic left by helicopter on the 15th whereas the rest left in a military convoy and went towards -- from Pale towards Serbia. At the beginning of the convoy or at the front of the convoy you had a Praga with a three-barrel -- with three barrels, and this was followed by the trucks with the families of those soldiers and at the rear there was another Praga and a three-barrelled device. And from that day on in the Rajlovac barracks there were not more than five officers who were waiting. They didn't have any transport or they were from other republics such as Macedonia, for example, or Montenegro. But as time went by, they left, too, and then we asked that our officers who were born in Bosnia, especially born on our territory, we asked have them sent, and so from August and September 1992 to the end of the war we wanted to have our military cadres and officers that were loyal to our lands, the lands that we had inhabited for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question was specifically about your military formations and the nature of the defence force as it was in the first month of the war, the defence force that you were a part of. Tell the Chamber something about the nature of the organisation of the defence force, how it rated with a modern army in your estimation, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, in Zabrdje we organised ourselves in the following way with people who lived in Zabrdje: In the Rajlovac barracks, people I said a moment ago who had come in from Brijesce to the Rajlovac barracks. And they set up a unit which had the strength of a company, and we in Zabrdje also established a unit which was of company strength. But even then we didn't have any special communications nor did we have battalions or brigades. We were not able to believe we were facing what we were facing. And as time went by until the army of Republika Srpska was formed, the situation improved militarily speaking and pursuant to the rules and regulations after military service, but until then we were a sort of village watch, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to what extent were the JNA supplying you with arms in that first month?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons we had were weapons we found in the barracks and those issued in March 1992. We didn't have any other weapons, nor did any other weapons come in to us, nor did I have any information that in those first months of the war that we needed any in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you some documents that we've got. Firstly, this bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Krsman, there appears to be two identical documents here, although they bear different Tribunal numbers, and they clearly are slightly different. One is a facsimile, and the other is not. They appear to say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour might want one numbered with an A and the other a B or something akin to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the -- the one with the TX report on the top would be then D155A, and the other would be D155B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's the one dated 9 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Firstly, had you seen this document before coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now you've had a chance to look at it, does it mean anything to you, bearing in mind the date?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a few moments ago I was talking about the attack launched by the Muslims on the 8th of May on my village and the surrounding parts, and from this date I can see that this is the 9th of May, which means that it was sent on -- prior to that to the European Community, which means that on the 8th of May the Muslims consciously made that ultimatum before attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what does this -- what did you understand this ultimatum to be?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here quite clearly, you can see that there are no Muslims from Sokolje. It says Muslims from Buljakov Potok, which mean the fringes of Sokolje, not towards Zabrdje but in-depth in their territory. And they had given an ultimatum to us, the Serbs of Rajlovac, and the Serbs from Sokolje Brdo, which means me, that we should cross over to their Muslim Territorial Defence, which is beyond belief. If it were not farcical it would be sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'd also like you to have a look, please, at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are again two documents here. Only one of them is relevant. In the English, it's the second -- although, in fact, it's page 4 of 6, where it begins "On the territory of the city of Sarajevo," and in the B/C/S I think it's on the last page, Mr. Krsman, and -- it's on the last page, the middle paragraph. And we see this is a report dated the 9th of May, 1992, signed in place of the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, from the Serb republic, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it says "On the territory of the city of Sarajevo, ferocious fighting has been repeated precisely in the region of the vicinity of Brijesce and the barracks in Rajlovac. Muslim paramilitary formations opened fire on the Serb forces and the innocent civilians. At the moment the fighting is ongoing but regarding the positions of the Serb forces and their maximum effort there is one military defeat of the Muslim extremists on the way." As a description of how the war started in Rajlovac, how accurate would you assess that to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The description is completely accurate, and they probably got this information from us, the report. So it's just as I had recounted it, that they attacked the whole of the Serb area, not only Rajlovac municipality but that it was a synchronised attack on all the areas around Sarajevo inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which consists of two documents. Mr. Josse, are we going to deal with the first one or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to me to have any relevance to this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we then consider to only take the document that is the second one? From what I understand we would then have in English --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The ERN number is ET02089406 to 02089409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. That would not be a good idea, Mr. Registrar, because that's the whole of the two documents. It would have those numbers, but it's only the last two pages of these numbers. That's 4 of 6 and 5 of 6, which covers the only of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's an academic point, but its not clear to me whether in fact this is one document. That is what the translator clearly assumed. That's why he or she has numbered the English 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep it simple. It consists of two documents, the first one irrelevant for the testimony of this witness. We keep it at D156. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Josse. Mr. Krsman, we'll have break until five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I do understand that you'd like to raise a procedural issue. Is the presence of the witness any problem in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to P1130, a document that came up during the course of the previous witness's testimony, there were four, I think, small translation errors noted. The Court asked for corrections to be provided. They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- have been -- have been corrected and the correct copies have been provided now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I promised I would give you an answer after the break that also caused us to have the break a little bit longer. We will not sit on the 29th. That means that it's fair to give compensation to the Defence for that missed day. You're supposed to finish by the 4th of April, so that the 5th of April will then compensate for the loss of the 29th of March. For reasons related to relative much time taken by the Bench for questioning -- or putting questions to witness, the Chamber finds it fair, perhaps I'll elaborate on that a bit more later, but finds it fair that a couple of days, we have calculated approximately how much time it took, that you give another few days. So that would mean that the 6th, the 7th, and the 10th of April, 10th of April is a Monday --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would then be available. And the Chamber then understood that since you are wanting to have Mr. Bjelica here to testify, that you would use those days. The Chamber would then assist to the best of its abilities to get Mr. Bjelica here on the 3rd of April, and then you having an opportunity to start, well, let's say the 6th or late bit 5th. It's also a matter of you using your time as efficiently as possible. Then the 11th of April we will reserve for miscellaneous matters, so if Bjelica would still need one more hour we might use the 11th, but there may be procedural issues. You would then have the 12th and the 13th as well as the 18th and the 19th of April available, four days' preparation for Mr. Krajisnik's testimony. You would have four consecutive days; that would, therefore, in the week before Easter and the Tuesday and the Wednesday after Easter. Then the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik would start on the 20th of April. And since you would have 20 days, from what I remember, that means that the examination-in-chief should be finished by the 17th [Realtime transcript read in error "27th"] of May, and then we'll continue. Of course, everything will be -- will move forward a tiny little bit. The thing I'd like to know -- yes. The transcript reads 20 -- yes, it's 17th of May that the -- yes. You would have to finish by the 16th as a matter of fact. If you start on a -- no. You start on Thursday the 20th of April. Twenty days would mean you have to finish your examination if chief by Wednesday the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I take it, in effect, everything is -- is moving on in correspondingly to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to that change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is what the Chamber suggests at this moment, and we're willing to give within the next five minutes -- we'd send a request to the Victims and Witnesses Section if you would agree to have Mr. Bjelica here if possible by the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, that would be extremely helpful that -- yes, thank you for that. Your Honour, may I just inquire because it's something that got crossed -- I'm sure the Trial Chamber doesn't want to spend time on it. But if I could just inquire, the -- all dates moving forward in accordance a these adjustments, that includes everything right to the very end, the Trial Chamber's judgement, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that next week, but we're considering the matter, and most likely we have to consider a few matters still, but most likely then a judgement would not be delivered before the summer recess because that becomes almost impossible on the basis already of the tight schedule. Then to what extent final briefs would have to be submitted before the summer recess. We still take it that it's before the summer recess. Whether the final -- whether we'll hear the final submissions by the parties still before the recess is uncertain, that we still have to work that out in more detail. We'll do that and we'll inform you by the beginning of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it may be obviously I don't want to take time this morning but is -- are both those elements, Your Honour, something on which there may be some submission and discussion about it in court? I'm talking about the lodging of final briefs. Is that a matter that could be revisited in court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're not going to spend days on it, but of course we'll listen to you before making final determinations in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The VWS is aware of what we're discussing at the moment, is following at this moment this hearing, and the VWS is requested to put every effort in getting Mr. Bjelica here by the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to go back a little bit in your evidence, Mr. Krsman, because there's something I forgot to ask you about, and it relates to the period after the laying of the minefield but before the outbreak of hostilities, and I want to ask you whether the certification of Zabrdje received any communication in that period from the Sokolje Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive any letters or mail. We had a direct telephone line that we used to communicate to each other about the activities that we were about to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, firstly perhaps you would tell the Chamber about this telephone line. Was it one that was specially commissioned?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The central post office was in Sarajevo. They switched off all the telephone lines save for this telephone line that connected our Crisis Staff and the Crisis Staff in Sokolje in question in which a person called Semso whose family name I don't know worked and we communicated with him. We negotiated with him, and everything was correct and up until the 7th of May when Semso called us and said, "People, I can no longer control the extremists here and I cannot guarantee you peace from this day on." And he said things would happen as they would happen. And he also informed us that the telephone line would be discontinued and that the previous agreements were no longer in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know what position Semso held in -- if any, in the Crisis Staff at Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semso was the head of a family in Sokolje who cooperated with us very well, and when he couldn't control these people he no longer had a position. There were other people? Positions, and they were in control, and what then meant was that they attacked us on the following day, on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before the break, I asked you something about the Serb formations at the outbreak of the war. What did you perceive of the Muslim formations in the first month of the war?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were observing the separation line, we noticed with our naked eye that they were digging their trenches and communicating trenches very fast. We called them by phone asking them why they were doing that, and they said for no reason, or they couldn't provide us with an adequate answer as to why they were doing that when we didn't do anything of the sort. In our village it was a very big problem when we had to tell people that we had to dig trenches on their property. At first they were not willing to do that, but later on as the war continued, we -- everybody realised that we had to reinforce our positions. They, on their part, started digging trenches as early as April. Their slogan was, "We will dig our way to freedom." It was a notorious fact. Everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to go into this -- invite you to go into this in a little more detail in a moment's time, but it's right, at the outbreak of hostilities you took up arms and fought for your side?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first attack, we established our defence line as best as we could. One has to be fair and say that at first we didn't see anybody during the first ten days. They were shooting at us from a distance. However, the shells were falling. We had to be very cautious. It was the very beginning of the war, and you have to know that before that none of us had heard a bullet being fired, and all of a sudden such a change without any training with elderly, with sick, with the children. We had had to try and survive. During the first six months we had the biggest number of casualties because we didn't know how to behave, how to defend ourselves from the enemy fire from -- from their bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the enemy fire in the first month or so that I want to ask you about. Were you able to make an assessment of the type of weaponry that your enemy had in the first one to two months of the war?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first month or so, save for the first day when we were being shelled by mortar, for the rest of the time they used only light weapons with an odd mortar shell here or there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any sort of cannons, artillery, that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the conflict escalated, they started using all sorts of equipment and weaponry, and I don't think that there is a piece of armament that they didn't use to shoot at us during the war. Cannons, tanks, howitzer, mortar. And also, you ever to bear in mind that there were those forces on Mount Igman that also fired on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a few discrete areas in relation to military activities in 1992. Firstly, you have described the nature of the formation of the Rajlovac defence forces in the first month or so of the war. After a month or two had passed, how did you organise yourself militarily? Briefly will suffice as far as I'm concerned in relation to this question.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, when the army of Republika Srpska was established, our companies joined up into a battalion. The Rajlovac battalion joined up another battalion and formed a brigade, the 2nd Battalion. And from then, that moment on, my duties were in my company. The battalion did its work. The brigade, it did its work. We behaved as any other classical military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You became a company commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your company known as?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of my company was the 3rd Company of Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were part of the Rajlovac Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were on the strength of the Rajlovac Brigade. There was another company composed of men from Brijesce, and there was another company composed of men from Reljevo, Cuca, Perivoj, which all belonged to the municipality of Rajlovac. The three companies that I've just mentioned made up this battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many men were in your company?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very outset there were 202 of us. Some died, some left. Some people who resided in town and had houses in Zabrdje joined us subsequently. Some men who married girls from Zabrdje were also ill-treated, so they joined us. When the war ended, I had 176 men on my strength, and that was more or less what our strength was in my company throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How were you selected as a -- or as the company commander?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was primarily chosen because I was relatively young. Everybody liked me and respected me as an honest and courageous lad. I was the president of the youth organisation. At that time it was very important to keep the danger at bay from young people. There was a meeting, and I was appointed the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Taking the second black and white map, could you indicate, please, where the front line was when the war commenced?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I show you the line that my company manned or the entire line of the Rajlovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The entire line would, I think, be more useful. Yes. Why don't you mark it on the map with a line.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the line, and below the minefield we -- on the previous map I indicated the minefields, and in my zone of responsibility we set up the line some 500 metres to a kilometre further, which largely depended on where we could defend ourselves better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I take it that your line, your company's line, was around the minefield?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Below the minefield. At some places 50 metres below it. At some, others up to a kilometre below the minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was the minefield effective as a -- protection?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minefield played its role primarily before the conflict broke out. The minefield was a psychological deterrent, so to speak. It is a well-known fact that a minefield works only if it is supervised. When we moved our line, the minefield was destroyed by game, by stray dogs - I'm talking about tripwire - and partly experts from the Muslim side came, cleared the minefield, took the mines away, used them for other things. This is what I subsequently heard. The minefield in question lost its function, and as the war progressed we set up new minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly. It's right that the line moved in a significant way in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to June 1993, in my village 37 people were killed. On the 12th of June, 1993, the Muslim formations launched a large-scale attack on Zabrdje in order to cut us off and join up with their unit in Visoko. The line was broken in depth of the territory in places up to three or four kilometres, and in other places it remained intact. And if you want me to, I can indicate what the new line looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For my purposes I don't need to ask you that question. Going back to 1992, I would like to ask you about whether there were any attacks on civilian targets in territory held by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, Zabrdje, in the zone of my responsibility, ten civilians were killed of whom seven women. Nine of them were killed by sniper fire, and one woman died in shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Give the Chamber some idea how far the snipers were shooting from.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it on this map. However, we were on elevation 484, which means that my village was in the valley. The enemy positions were on elevation 585 to 599 and even higher up. The height difference was between 80 and a hundred metres. The complete line that I indicated on the map was below them. All the time there have been stories that we were shooting from a hill. However, there are witnesses and the map shows it that this was not the case. Our line was between 50 and 200 metres, and you could see with the naked eye who is a civilian and who is a fighter. Out of the ten deaths of civilians in my village, I found myself in eight of these cases, and I assisted in their transportation. On the 12th of June, a grandmother called Mirka Mijatovic died during an attack. The other nine cases were people who were killed by sniper fire during a cease-fire. They were killed by a single bullet. No other bullets were fired. If you want me to, I can even give you the exact dates when those deaths happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, the question simply was from what distance were snipers shooting. Mr. Josse, of course if you want to take your time and let the witness tell us two minutes whether it was one bullet and other things instead of insisting on getting an answer to your question, it's your time. Please proceed. So could you please tell us from what distance snipers were shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The snipers were shooting from a distance of between 50 to 200 metres depending on the location they were shooting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You made reference to a lady, Ms. Mijatovic, being killed on the 12th of June. 12th of June of what year, please?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12th of June, 1993, when that attack was launched on Zabrdje and when half the village fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to lead the witness on those matters contained in the bottom of the penultimate page of the 65 ter going to the top of the following page. If the Chamber and my learned friend won't permit me to lead, I'll ask the witness to deal with it by way of recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether or not Mr. Tieger opposes, but please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that -- right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is right that you recall a lady called Jovanka Krsman being killed by a bullet on the 8th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my aunt, and on Women's Day, the 8th of March, she made us a cup of coffee to celebrate the day. She went outside to bring us the coffee, and she was hit by a direct sniper hit in the middle of her forehead. And otherwise there wasn't a single bullet being shot. It was -- there was a truce, a cease-fire. The sniper had to know that this was a woman civilian. She was tall. She was wearing a skirt. And that is a classical example of a crime having been committed, or how else shall I call it? We managed to pull her out but it was too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May of 1993, Darinka Micukic who was shot by a bullet to the heart. I don't think we need the details, Mr. Krsman. Just "yes" if you agree with what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day it was a truce again. Just one bullet was fired, Darinka Micukic, a woman, got hit in the middle of her heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ms. Mijatovic, who you've mentioned, was struck by a mortar on the 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her fate was somewhat different. She just happened to be there when a shell fell, which means that they shot intentionally, but she just happened to be along that way and the shell hit her and killed her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A lady called Ms. Lemez was killed by a cannon round in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her house was near the front line, about a hundred metres from the front line. And once again, a shell hit her and her body was dispersed. We couldn't even recognise her when we saw her. She went out to tend to her cow. There was a truce in force, a sort of truce at the time. Her son was president of the SDS later on after the late Bora Bjeljac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally, in mid-1994 a woman called Koviljka Krajisnik was killed by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five days before her, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik's father was wounded. We never mentioned that. It was a light wound, but it was the same sniper who five days later -- well, Koviljka Krajisnik lived at Pale. She'd come down to fetch some documents from the house. She'd left because the front line was there after the fall of Zabrdje, and the sniper shot just one bullet which hit her in the heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And she is as far as you are aware is the wife of Mr. Krajisnik's, the accused's, first cousin?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and their houses were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to turn to a different subject, please, and that is the barracks. What happened to the barracks in 1992? What use was made of them?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, when the Yugoslav People's Army left, the barracks were taken over, first of all, by the people who lived across the road in Brijesce, that is to say Serbs who had left their homes in fear of an attack by the Muslim extremists. But as time went by, it began to fill up with people who were fleeing Sarajevo. And you can see there's a large meadow and most of them came in across that meadow. And the greatest exodus took place on the 17th of May from the Pofalici settlement, which is a Serb settlement in the town which was attacked by Muslim units. And so they went across Zuci, Perivoj, and Dvor, and arrived at the barracks, and there were about 3.000 of them, women, children, elderly people. The entire settlement had escaped. Part of them stayed on in the barracks. The women and children fled in different directions, so the barracks quite literally served as a collective centre because it was a very large barracks with a lot of facilities, a large kitchen, everything else that a barracks would have. So we used it for defence answer as a collective -- collection centre for people who didn't have anywhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What sort of numbers of people are we talking about in terms of those who didn't have anywhere else to go?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a realistic figure would be about 4 to 500 people. Sometimes there were more, sometimes less. It varied. There were other units as the army began to be established, so others went off to other units, but mostly -- well, there were two companies there, 200 men, and add another 200 to that, people working in the kitchen, civilians who worked in the washing area and so on. So about 500 people when the battlefield stabilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And other than these military personnel and those who were assisting them, support staff, cooks, for example, were there any other occupants of the barracks or the outbuildings connected with the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any other people, just the ones I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At any point were there civilians there?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were civilians, but we never referred to them it as civilians because it was the front line. So the women who worked in the kitchen and those working in the laundry, they had their wartime assignments. So there weren't any civilians in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in terms of attacks on the barracks, did that occur and, if so, how were you able to defend the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks, well, it was a targeting area because it was under Sokolje. And for the first year of the war, 200 people were killed, about 200 people killed in the barracks, and a far larger number were wounded. And they never attack the barracks as an infantry because they thought it was well mined and well fortified. They always tried to do it in a different way. And you can see our last defence line, they tried to attack that through Zabrdje on three occasions but they never succeeded, if you look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any member of the Rajlovac brigade stopping a humanitarian convoy?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a checkpoint where my company met the other company. It was along the main road Visoko running to Sarajevo. That was the checkpoint.
